articles.title: Liquid AI Ships LFM2.5-2.6B: An On-Device Agentic Model With 128K Context and Tool Calling
articles.tldr: Liquid AI released LFM2.5-2.6B, a 2.69B parameter agentic model that runs entirely on-device. It has a 128K context window, native tool calling, and was pre-trained on ~34 trillion tokens. Two checkpoints shipped: a base model for fine-tuning and a post-trained model for agentic workloads. It decodes at 220 tokens/s on an M5 Max in under 2.5 GB of memory.
articles.why_it_matters: On-device agentic models change the economics and privacy equation for AI-powered tools. At 2.6B parameters with tool calling, LFM2.5 can run agentic workflows on phones, laptops, and edge devices with zero API costs and no data leaving the device. Day-one support in llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and LM Studio means it drops into existing local inference stacks immediately.

Day-one support in llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and LM Studio

articles.title: GPT-5.6 August Update: OpenAI Rolls Out Improved Sol and Luna With Effort Slider
articles.tldr: OpenAI released updated GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna models in ChatGPT, replacing GPT-5.5 Instant as the default for Free and Go users. Plus and Pro users get an effort slider to control how much reasoning ChatGPT applies per response. Both models are rated High capability in Cybersecurity and Biological/Chemical domains under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework. The July versions remain in Codex and ChatGPT Work.
articles.why_it_matters: The effort slider is the practical takeaway: it lets developers and power users trade latency for depth on a per-query basis, rather than switching between models. For engineers using ChatGPT as a daily tool, this means fast answers for simple questions and deep reasoning for complex debugging — without model-switching friction. The High cybersecurity capability rating also signals these models are increasingly useful for security-adjacent engineering work.

articles.title: Microsoft Research Releases Orchard: Open-Source Agentic AI Where 3B Params Hits 69.7% on SWE-bench
articles.tldr: Microsoft Research released Orchard, an open-source framework for scalable agentic AI research. Built around Orchard Env, a reusable Kubernetes environment service, it supports training and evaluating agents across software engineering, web navigation, and personal assistant domains. Orchard-SWE reaches 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified (73.0% with reranking) using only ~3B active parameters — approaching frontier systems 10x larger.
articles.why_it_matters: A 3B parameter model hitting 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified challenges the assumption that you need frontier-scale models for effective coding agents. The framework trains agents inside real deployment harnesses (Codex, OpenClaw), not sandboxed toy environments. For teams building custom coding agents, this provides a reproducible training pipeline with open data, open weights, and open evaluation — no proprietary infrastructure required.

articles.title: First Production-Scale Study of Coding Agents: 3.2M Users, 95 Trillion Tokens From GitHub Copilot
articles.tldr: Microsoft Research published the first production-scale characterization of agentic coding workloads using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026: 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens. Key finding: KV cache hit rates average 90% within a turn but drop to 55% across turn boundaries. They built an idle-time predictor that captures 86-90% of total idle time for resource orchestration.
articles.why_it_matters: This paper provides the empirical foundation for building agent-native infrastructure. The finding that KV cache invalidates dramatically at turn boundaries means current LLM serving systems — designed for chatbots — are architecturally mismatched for coding agents. The 1:1 coupling of LLM calls to tool execution and the long-tailed token consumption patterns suggest we need fundamentally different serving infrastructure for agents.
traction_evidence: Published by Microsoft Research (arXiv, July 2026)
Based on production GitHub Copilot data — 3.2M users
First study of its kind at this scale
761M LLM calls and 95T tokens analyzed

use_cases: Designing LLM serving infrastructure optimized for agentic workloads

articles.title: JetBrains Opens IntelliJ's Java and Kotlin Intelligence Via LSP for VS Code, Cursor, and Agents
articles.tldr: JetBrains released a preview VS Code extension that brings IntelliJ IDEA's Java and Kotlin language intelligence to VS Code, Cursor, and other LSP-capable editors via the Language Server Protocol. The extension includes smart completion, navigation, code analysis, refactorings, and debugging. Internal trials show the same LSP functionality significantly improves terminal-based agentic workflows like Claude Code and Codex.
articles.why_it_matters: This is JetBrains acknowledging that developers are splitting time between IDEs and agentic flows. By exposing IntelliJ's battle-tested Java/Kotlin intelligence as an LSP server, coding agents get deterministic language understanding — type-aware navigation, refactoring, and analysis — instead of relying on LLMs to infer code structure. For Java/Kotlin teams, this means their coding agents get the same quality of code intelligence that IntelliJ users have had for years.

articles.title: Vercel Ships Agent Plugins 1.0: A Standard Format for Packaging Agent Skills and MCP Servers
articles.tldr: Vercel released Agent Plugins 1.0, an open, vendor-neutral standard for packaging Agent Skills and MCP servers into distributable plugins. A plugin is a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for skills and MCP configurations. The format is intentionally minimal — clients handle installation, distribution, and UX. Compatible clients include Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others.
articles.why_it_matters: Agent Skills and MCP servers are reusable, but every client packages and discovers them differently. Agent Plugins gives extension authors one format instead of adapting the same component for every client. This is the npm-for-agent-tools moment: a shared packaging standard means skills and MCP servers can be distributed, versioned, and discovered across the ecosystem without client-specific rewrites.

1.0.0 specification publicly available at agent-plugins.org
Vendor-neutral — works across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex

Building an ecosystem of reusable agent extensions

articles.title: Temporal Releases Deputy: Open-Source Supply Chain Security Toolchain Built With AI Agents
articles.tldr: Temporal released Deputy, an open-source, CLI-first security toolchain for inventorying, scanning, triaging, and controlling dependencies across repositories, container images, VM disk images, and SBOMs. It provides a shared, customizable policy layer for local use, CI, and download-time enforcement. Built using Claude Code and Codex, Deputy also puts deterministic supply chain guardrails around AI-assisted development.
articles.why_it_matters: Supply chain attacks are accelerating (see this week's Keyv/Shai-Hulud compromise), and existing scanners drown teams in false positives. Deputy addresses both: deterministic analysis with customizable policies, plus guardrails specifically designed for AI-generated code and dependencies. Coming from Temporal's security team — who built it for their own estate — it's production-tested, not theoretical.

articles.title: How Duolingo Built a Production-Ready Agent Platform: Define Once, Run Everywhere
articles.tldr: Duolingo published a detailed engineering blog on how they built a shared agent platform to stop teams from repeatedly rebuilding the same infrastructure. Agents are defined in a registry (system prompt, MCP servers, repo access), and the platform handles execution, orchestration, observability, and evaluation. Agents are invokable across Slack, internal sites, CLI, and Temporal workflows without rebuilding per surface.
articles.why_it_matters: Every company deploying AI agents hits the same wall Duolingo did: prototyping is easy, productionizing is the problem. Their solution — a registry-based platform with shared execution, multi-surface distribution, and built-in observability — is the blueprint for how mid-to-large engineering orgs should operationalize agents. The explicit separation of agent definition from infrastructure is the key architectural decision.

articles.title: ByteDance Deer-Flow Crosses 79K GitHub Stars: The Long-Horizon SuperAgent Harness
articles.tldr: ByteDance's Deer-Flow, an open-source long-horizon SuperAgent harness, has crossed 79,000 GitHub stars. It handles tasks ranging from minutes to hours using sandboxes, persistent memory, tools, skills, subagents, and a message gateway. The framework is designed for research, coding, and creative tasks that require sustained autonomous operation.
articles.why_it_matters: At 79K stars, Deer-Flow has quietly become one of the most popular agent frameworks on GitHub. Its focus on long-horizon tasks — the kind that take hours, not seconds — addresses the gap between quick coding assists and sustained autonomous engineering. The combination of sandboxes, persistent memory, and subagent orchestration is the infrastructure pattern that long-running agent workflows require.

use_cases: Long-horizon autonomous coding and research tasks

articles.title: Kubeflow SDK Crosses 1 Million PyPI Downloads: One Import for Training, Tuning, and Registry
articles.tldr: The unified kubeflow-sdk package crossed 1 million PyPI downloads, consolidating what used to be separate SDKs for kubeflow-training, kubeflow-katib, and model-registry into a single pip install kubeflow. The SDK abstracts Kubernetes complexity so ML engineers can go from local prototype to distributed training without rewriting code, rebuilding containers, or writing YAML.
articles.why_it_matters: ML infrastructure has been notoriously fragmented — different tools for training, tuning, serving, and model management. The unified SDK reaching 1M downloads signals that the community has converged on a single interface. For teams running ML workloads on Kubernetes, this eliminates the context-switching between separate SDKs and the boilerplate of translating local code to distributed training configurations.
